column1: What are the five fundamental invariants of interior spatial composition?
column2: 1) Every space has a primary organizing axis; 2) Proportion systems establish visual harmony; 3) Circulation patterns are movement choreography; 4) Spatial hierarchy establishes zones of purpose; 5) Scale relationships govern legibility of form.

column1: How does interior design fundamentally differ from architecture in terms of their relationship to space?
column2: Architecture defines the container (the bounded volume itself), while interior design works within an already-bounded volume, transforming that void into a coherent, navigable, emotionally resonant environment.

column1: Who formalized proxemics, and what are the four concentric zones identified?
column2: Edward T. Hall (1960s). The four zones: intimate distance (skin contact to ~18 inches), personal distance (18 inches to 4 feet), social distance (4 to 12 feet), and public distance (beyond 12 feet).

column1: Why are proxemic zones considered biological invariants rather than cultural constructs?
column2: They reflect hardwired neural circuitry governing threat assessment and social bonding—violating intimate distance without permission triggers amygdala-driven stress hormone cascades regardless of conscious rationalization.

column1: What is the biomechanical consequence of a countertop height of 39 inches for a standing adult?
column2: It forces most standing adults into chronic thoracic flexion, compressing intervertebral discs and straining the erector spinae muscle group.

column1: What are the three irreducible domains governing human-centered spatial design?
column2: Anthropometrics (skeletal/dimensional constraints), proxemics (social spatial buffering), and sensory-cognitive coupling (bidirectional feedback between environment and neural processing).

column1: What is the core invariant principle of material systems thinking in interior design?
column2: Every material has authentic properties and authentic limits—no material can simultaneously be the cheapest, most durable, most sustainable, most thermally efficient, AND most aesthetically flexible. Trade-offs are permanent.

column1: How do a polished concrete floor and a cork-tiled version of the same slab differ in performance?
column2: Polished concrete behaves as a reflective, thermally massive heat sink; cork tile over the same slab becomes a warm, compliant, acoustically absorptive surface—demonstrating how finish transforms tectonic performance.

column1: What is the foundational invariant of interior design methodology regarding how space is experienced?
column2: Space is experienced sequentially through time, not statically from a single vantage point—designers must orchestrate temporal progression via threshold transitions, sightline choreography, and material shifts.

column1: What anthropometric rationale explains the standard 18-inch seat depth?
column2: It corresponds to the femur length from hip joint to knee, making it a physiological requirement rather than a stylistic preference.

column1: What does a 36-inch minimum hallway width accommodate, and why is this dimension non-negotiable?
column2: It accommodates human shoulder breadth plus a gesture envelope; violating this dimension produces measurable physical discomfort since it derives from fixed body biomechanics, not aesthetic choice.

column1: What three frameworks structure material systems analysis in interior design?
column2: 1) Physical properties taxonomy (measurable performance attributes); 2) Tectonic expression and constructability (how materials assemble and interface); 3) Lifecycle thinking (environmental and economic commitment beyond initial installation).
